Lesson 7 · Guided route

From prediction to intervention: guided case

Would offering a new team tool improve performance?

Follow the manager’s request through the evidence, a worked step in the analysis, and a practical next action. The business case gives the decision at a glance; the technical appendix takes the method further.

Business caseTechnical appendix
Story chapters
  1. 01. A popular tool appears to work
  2. 02. Separate selection from improvement
  3. 03. Run a pilot tied to the budget

Part 1 of 3

A popular tool appears to work

A team-performance manager sees that teams using a new tool score much higher than teams that do not. The observed gap is 15.08 outcome units, large enough to make a rollout sound obvious. Yet managers chose which teams received the tool. High-performing teams may have been more likely to adopt it in the first place.

The business question is not whether users outperform nonusers. It is whether offering the tool changes outcomes enough to justify its cost. That question needs an action, a time window, a stable team unit, and a measure of performance that would matter to management.

A rollout meeting should separate three groups that are easy to blur: teams offered the tool, teams that actually use it, and teams that would have performed well anyway. The last group cannot be identified from observed scores alone. Without that distinction, the firm might spend its budget on a tool that merely happened to reach its strongest teams first.

Part 2 of 3

Separate selection from improvement

The observed gap contains two pieces: how recipients would have performed without the tool, and what the tool changed for them. The case lets the manager separate those pieces. The large user-versus-nonuser gap shrinks once selection is accounted for, changing the purchase discussion.

How this number is built

Define the treatment as an offer to an eligible team. The current user-versus-nonuser comparison combines the effect on recipients with their starting advantage. That is why a pilot should compare teams by assigned offer rather than by who chose to use the tool.

Worked step: Observed user gap = 15.08 outcome units. Conceptually, that gap = the tool’s gain for recipients + the difference those teams would have shown without it. A randomized offer aims to make the second component average out across groups.

Keep the assignment list, outcome window, and adoption record. The offer comparison answers the purchase question; adoption explains whether the proposed rollout can be delivered.

See the full method in the appendix →

For an actual decision, the manager would assign the offer randomly among eligible teams, keep usual operations as the comparison, and measure the same outcome over the same period. The primary result would compare teams by offer, including those that barely use the tool; usage can be studied separately.

Random assignment does not make every team identical; it makes the groups comparable in expectation before outcomes are seen. Managers should keep the assignment record even if some teams decline the offer, because changing groups after observing use would reintroduce selection. Adoption and ease of implementation are still useful secondary outcomes for planning a full rollout.

Part 3 of 3

Run a pilot tied to the budget

A pilot should name the minimum gain that repays license fees, training time, and workflow disruption. If the expected gain is smaller than that threshold, a statistically positive result may still be a poor purchase. If the gain clears it, management can expand gradually while checking whether the tool works for teams outside the pilot.

The pilot record needs the assignment list, dates, adoption rates, outcome definition, and reasons for missing teams. Without those practical details, a clean-looking difference could be hard to interpret or repeat.

The budget threshold should be written in the same units as the outcome: what gain per team would cover licenses, training and management attention? If a pilot misses that threshold, the firm can investigate whether the tool was poorly used or whether the benefit is simply too small. Either conclusion is more useful than treating the original user-versus-nonuser gap as a purchase order.

Decision check

What does the 15-unit user-versus-nonuser gap leave unresolved?

Compare your reasoning

It does not show how much the tool changed recipients’ outcomes. Team selection contributed to the gap.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The generator stores both potential outcomes. Its average effect among recipients is 4.58; its average effect across all teams is 2.42. Those are different targets.

The bigger picture

A business can predict which teams will do well and still be uncertain whether buying a tool will help them. The purchase decision calls for a comparison of what happens with and without an offer, tied to a budget threshold. A planned pilot makes that comparison part of the rollout rather than an afterthought. The wider lesson applies to training, software, incentives, and service changes: define the intervention and the gain needed to justify it before expansion. The next lesson tackles the same decision when an experiment was not built into the program.
